summary: Proposes RA-Guard, a lightweight way to block unwanted IPv6 Router Advertisements by filtering in the layer-2 network fabric, as an alternative or complement to Secure Neighbor Discovery. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A guard at a door of the network checks who is allowed to say they are the router and turns away impostors.

questions: how to block rogue router advertisements
does ra guard work with send
subtitle: Letting the switches on a shared IPv6 link drop router announcements that do not come from real routers.

tldr.problem: On a shared layer-2 segment, an unauthorized or misconfigured router can send rogue Router Advertisements, and Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) is hard to deploy everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: RA-Guard has the layer-2 device check each incoming Router Advertisement against rules such as port, link-layer address, source address or prefix list, or against SEND validation, and forward or drop it.
tldr.outcome: It is a light-weight alternative and complement to SEND, but it only works when all traffic crosses controlled layer-2 devices. The RFC is Informational and was later updated by RFC 7113.

facts.label: Stateless criteria
facts.value: Link-layer address, port, IP source address, prefix list

today: RFC 6105 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7113, so read the two together.

sections.title: The Rogue Router Advertisement Problem
sections.content:
On a shared layer-2 (L2) network segment, devices announce themselves as routers by sending Router Advertisements (RAs). If not every device supports Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971), or the infrastructure for SEND is missing, an unauthorized or badly configured router can send rogue RAs, either maliciously or by accident. That causes operational problems for the hosts on the segment.

RFC 6105 describes a solution framework for the rogue-RA problem described in RFC 6104. It targets segments built around one or more L2 switching devices that can recognise invalid RAs and block them. Solutions in the framework range from basic, where a port is statically told to forward or not forward RAs, to advanced, where the switch validates each RA dynamically, even using SEND.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine anyone in a classroom could shout 'I am the teacher, follow me!' RA-Guard is a helper who only lets the real teacher's voice through.

sections.title: Model and Applicability
sections.content:
RA-Guard applies where all messages between IPv6 end devices pass through the controlled L2 devices. It does not apply to shared media where devices can talk directly without going through an RA-Guard-capable L2 device. In the RFC's Figure 1, the L2 device blocks incoming RAs from hosts and allows them from the router.

The RFC says RA-Guard is not a substitute for SEND. It is meant to complement SEND where SEND is unsuitable or not supported by every device, for example some IPv6-enabled sensors. It can be seen as a superset of SEND for router authorization: criteria run from "RA disallowed on a given interface" through "RA allowed from pre-defined sources" to "RA allowed from authorized sources only".

RA-Guard also introduces a router authorization proxy. Instead of every node judging each RA, a legitimate node in the middle does the check on behalf of all nodes on the link. An L2 device does not change the content of a validated RA, so it avoids the pitfalls of ND proxies. With SEND-based RA-Guard, only the L2 switch and the routers need certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every kid checking whether the teacher is real, one hall monitor checks for everybody. This only works if all the kids have to walk past the monitor.

sections.title: Stateless RA-Guard
sections.content:
Stateless RA-Guard decides whether to forward or block an RA using only the message itself and the configuration of the L2 device. The information in a received frame that can be used includes the link-layer address of the sender, the port it arrived on, the IP source address and the prefix list.

The device can be configured with allowed or disallowed link-layer addresses, ports and IP source addresses, an allowed prefix list and prefix ranges, and a router priority. If the RA matches the configuration it is forwarded, whether unicast or multicast. Otherwise it is dropped.

The simplest example is a small L2 switch where one interface is statically configured as the router-facing interface. Only that interface forwards RAs, and all non-router interfaces block them.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard has a written list at the door. If you are on the list, you come in. If not, you are turned away.

sections.title: Stateful RA-Guard and Its States
sections.content:
Stateful RA-Guard learns legitimate RA senders dynamically and remembers them. In a simple scheme the L2 device listens to RAs for a manually configured period, then allows later RAs only on ports where valid RAs were received during that period. The LEARNING state is often started by hand when a new IPv6 router is provisioned.

When RA-Guard uses a discovery method, it has four states. OFF means the capability is not in use. LEARNING means the device is acquiring information about attached routers, either blocking all RAs or temporarily forwarding all of them until they are verified. BLOCKING blocks ingress RAs. FORWARDING accepts valid ingress RAs and forwards them.

At the end of LEARNING, each interface moves to BLOCKING if no valid router was found on it, or to FORWARDING if one was. An operator can move an interface between BLOCKING and FORWARDING directly, and either state can return to LEARNING on operator instruction or a triggered event. When RA-Guard is SEND-based, the state machine is per-peer and defined in RFC 3971.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard first spends some time watching who the real teacher is. After that, he lets that teacher's voice through and blocks everyone else.

sections.title: SEND-Based RA-Guard
sections.content:
In the SEND-based variant the L2 device verifies each captured RA using SEND. It first verifies the Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA) and the RSA signature as specified in RFC 3971, and drops the RA if that fails. It then looks for a valid certificate for the public key in its cache. If one is found, the RA is forwarded.

If not, the device sends a Certification Path Solicitation (CPS) with an unspecified source address, captures the Certification Path Advertisement (CPA) and tries to validate the certificate chain. Failure means the RA is dropped. Success means the RA is forwarded and the certificate is cached.

The L2 device should be provisioned with a trust anchor certificate. It may also need layer-3 connectivity to a CRL Certification Path Advertisement server and an NTP server. The RFC suggests solving this bootstrapping issue by configuring a trusted port toward a first router, and using SEND-based RA-Guard on all other ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard asks the speaker for an ID card signed by someone he trusts. No valid card means no entry, and he remembers the cards he has already checked.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
RA-Guard is effective only when all messages between IPv6 devices pass through controlled L2 devices. With Ethernet hubs, devices can communicate directly, and RA-Guard cannot protect against rogue RAs. It also offers no protection where IPv6 traffic is tunneled.

The Security Considerations section says that once the criteria are set up, and if the filter follows them strictly, legitimate RAs are not accidentally filtered. It stresses that the LEARNING state should only be entered intentionally by manual configuration, and that the network manager should check the list of learned routers against the expected valid list. That way both accidental and intentional rogue RAs are blocked.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard only works if everyone has to walk past him. If kids can sneak around through a side door, he cannot help.
